catalog_quote: 5. PROSODIC FEATURES The present analysis of the prosodic features is tentative pending further investigation of the interrelation of tone, stress and higher level phonology with intonation patterns. ... 5.2 The prosodic features of pitch and force work together to produce a feature of 'accent'. The syllable with the strongest force receives high pitch. Only two pitch patterns occur on di-syllabic words ... and three patterns on three syllable words ... Four syllable words combine the pitch/stress patterns which occur on di-syllabic words in various sequences ... Neither high pitch, low pitch nor stress is predictable by any outside criterion. No words have yet been observed which are minimally different in terms of either pitch or stress. Many words when pronounced in isolation fluctuate in their pitch/stress pattern. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on p.17 (sec. 5.2) of the Davis 1969 scan we hold, confirmed against both the djvu scanned and the page render; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1969 phonology article in Linguistics by the SIL fieldworker -- the only phonology Glottolog 5.1 lists for want1252 and the source WALS 13A also relies on; nothing newer on Wantoat prosody surfaced in a full scan of Glottolog's sources.bib (silpng/sil16 included), the held StressTyp2 dump (no Wantoat lect), Quigley 2003's Wantoat-family bibliography, or McElhanon 1973 (downloaded now; silent on stress). So the best available description is held and quoted.
